analogy.p: Think of a bit as a single sock, a byte as a box that holds exactly 8 socks, and each bigger unit as a bigger container that holds 1000 of the one before: a lorry (megabyte) holds 1000 crates (kilobytes), and so on. To work out how much space your house move needs, you count the items (pixels, samples or characters), multiply by how many socks each item needs (colour depth, bit depth or bits per character), then convert the total number of socks into boxes and lorries. The analogy breaks down because real computers do not count in whole lorries: the same data can be shown as 1000-based or 1024-based units, and a socks-in-boxes model cannot show that files also carry extra metadata.
analogy.t: Packing boxes for a house move

bullets: Know the **units in order** and the size of each: bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.
Be able to **convert** between bits, bytes and the larger units by multiplying or dividing by 8 or 1000.
Be able to **calculate the file size** of an image (width × height × colour depth), a sound file (sample rate × bit depth × duration) and a text file (bits per character × number of characters).
Be able to work out **how much storage is needed** for a set of files, or how many files will fit on a device.
Know how changing **resolution, colour depth, sample rate, bit depth or duration** changes the file size, and what that does to quality.
Always give an **answer with the correct unit** and show your working, because the mark scheme awards method marks.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.2 (Memory and storage) requires you to know the **units of data storage** (bit, nibble, byte, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte, petabyte), to **convert between those units**, and to **calculate the file size and storage capacity needed** for text, images and sound. It sits beside the 'data representation' content on binary, characters, images and sound, because you cannot calculate a file size until you know how many bits each character, pixel or sound sample uses. This is a very reliable source of marks on Paper 1: calculation questions are usually 2 to 4 marks and the method marks are easy to collect if you set the working out clearly.

bullets: A **bit** is a single binary digit, either 0 or 1; it is the **smallest unit of data**.
Computers use binary because electronic components are **two-state devices** (on/off, high/low voltage), which is cheap, fast and reliable.
Bits are grouped so they can represent more: a group of **n bits can represent 2^n different values**.
All file types (text, images, sound, video, programs) are ultimately stored as **sequences of bits**.
File size and device capacity are measured in the same units, so you can compare them directly (does the file **fit** on the device?).
core.h: Why storage is measured in bits and bytes
core.p: A computer stores everything (programs, text, pictures, sound) as **binary**, a pattern of 0s and 1s. This is because the hardware is made of billions of tiny switches (transistors) that have only two reliable states: on and off. A single 0 or 1 is called a **bit** (short for binary digit), and it is the smallest unit of data a computer can store. Because one bit on its own can only represent two things, bits are grouped together so that more complicated information can be stored. Every storage and memory device (RAM, hard disk, SSD, USB stick) has a capacity measured in these units, which is why you need to be able to compare and calculate with them.

bullets: **1 bit** = a single 0 or 1.
**1 nibble** = 4 bits.
**1 byte** = 8 bits.
**1 kilobyte (KB)** = 1000 bytes.
**1 megabyte (MB)** = 1000 kilobytes (1 000 000 bytes).
**1 gigabyte (GB)** = 1000 megabytes (1 000 000 000 bytes).
**1 terabyte (TB)** = 1000 gigabytes, and **1 petabyte (PB)** = 1000 terabytes.
Order of size, smallest to largest: **bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB**.
core.h: The units of data storage in order
core.p: You must know the order and the size of each unit. Starting from the bit, each unit is made by grouping the one before it. A **nibble** is 4 bits (half a byte, and the amount needed to write one hexadecimal digit). A **byte** is 8 bits, which is enough to store one character in extended ASCII. After the byte the OCR specification works in steps of **1000**: a kilobyte is 1000 bytes, a megabyte is 1000 kilobytes, and so on up to the petabyte. A handy way to remember the order is that each prefix is 1000 times bigger than the one before: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta.

bullets: **Bits to bytes:** divide by 8 (for example 64 000 bits ÷ 8 = 8000 bytes).
**Bytes to bits:** multiply by 8 (for example 50 bytes × 8 = 400 bits).
**Bytes to KB:** divide by 1000; **KB to MB:** divide by 1000; **MB to GB:** divide by 1000.
**GB to MB:** multiply by 1000 (for example 2.5 GB × 1000 = 2500 MB).
**Nibbles to bits:** multiply by 4; **bytes to nibbles:** multiply by 2.
A quick check: if you are going **up** the units your number should get **smaller**; if it does not, you have multiplied when you should have divided.
Convert **all values to the same unit** before comparing them (for example change 1.5 GB to 1500 MB before comparing with a 900 MB file).
core.p: To convert between units you either multiply or divide. The rule is simple: **going to a smaller unit gives a bigger number (multiply)** because you need more of the small units to make the same amount, and **going to a bigger unit gives a smaller number (divide)**. The only step that is not 1000 is between bits and bytes, which is **8**. Almost every file-size calculation first produces a number of bits, so the usual sequence is: bits ÷ 8 = bytes, bytes ÷ 1000 = KB, KB ÷ 1000 = MB, MB ÷ 1000 = GB. Write each conversion on its own line so that the marker can see the method even if you make an arithmetic slip.

bullets: OCR J277 uses **1 KB = 1000 bytes** as the standard conversion.
Some systems use **1 KB = 1024 bytes** (2^10); the correct name for 1024 bytes is a **kibibyte (KiB)**.
**Always follow any conversion given in the question**, even if it is 1024.
The difference grows with size: 1 GB (1000^3 bytes) is about **7% smaller** than 1 GiB (1024^3 bytes).
This explains why a '1 TB' drive appears as about **931 GiB** on some operating systems.
In answers, state the conversion you are using (for example 'using 1 KB = 1000 bytes') so method marks are protected.
core.p: There are two systems in use. In the **decimal (SI) system**, which OCR uses in its specification and which the mark scheme expects unless told otherwise, kilo means 1000. However, because computer memory is addressed in binary, some operating systems and textbooks use 1024 (which is 2^10) instead. The strict names for the 1024 system are **kibibyte (KiB), mebibyte (MiB) and gibibyte (GiB)**. This is why a drive sold as '500 GB' may be shown by an operating system as slightly less: the manufacturer counts in 1000s, the software counts in 1024s. In an exam, use **1000** unless the question gives you a different conversion; if it says 1 KB = 1024 bytes, follow the question.

bullets: **Colours:** a colour depth of n bits gives 2^n possible colours (1-bit = 2, 8-bit = 256, 24-bit = 16 777 216).
**Characters:** 7-bit ASCII gives 128 characters; 8-bit extended ASCII gives 256; Unicode uses more bits per character so it can represent characters from **all the world's languages**.
To find the bits needed for 200 colours: 2^7 = 128 is too few, 2^8 = 256 is enough, so **8 bits** are needed.
Adding **one** bit doubles the number of values but only **adds** to the file size by a fixed amount per item.
Link to topic 1.2 binary: this is exactly why binary patterns are limited in length.
core.h: How many different values can n bits store?
core.p: Each extra bit **doubles** the number of different patterns you can make, because every existing pattern can now end in either a 0 or a 1. So **n bits can store 2^n different values**. This is the key link between storage and data representation: it tells you how many colours an image can use, how many characters a character set can hold, and how many sound levels a sample can distinguish. To find the number of bits needed for a given number of values, find the smallest power of 2 that is **at least** that large.

bullets: **File size (bits) = bits per character × number of characters.**
ASCII uses **7 bits per character** (128 characters), often stored in **8 bits (1 byte)**; use the number the question gives.
**Unicode** uses more bits per character, so the same text takes more space but supports many more symbols and languages.
**Count every character**, including spaces and punctuation, unless the question says otherwise.
Example: 2500 characters × 8 bits = 20 000 bits ÷ 8 = 2500 bytes = **2.5 KB**.
In an 8-bit system, the file size in **bytes equals the number of characters**, a useful shortcut to check your answer.
core.h: Calculating the size of a text file
core.p: Text is stored by giving every character its own binary code from a **character set** such as ASCII or Unicode. The file size is therefore the **number of characters multiplied by the number of bits used for each character**. Spaces, punctuation, numbers and line breaks all count as characters. The answer comes out in bits, so you convert to bytes and then to KB. A document that uses a character set with more bits per character (such as Unicode) is bigger than the same text in ASCII, but it can hold a much wider range of characters.

bullets: **Pixel** = the smallest single element of a bitmap image; each has a binary colour value.
**Colour depth** = the number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel; more bits means more possible colours.
**Resolution** = the number of pixels in the image (width × height); higher resolution means more detail but a larger file.
**File size (bits) = width × height × colour depth**, then ÷ 8 for bytes.
**Metadata** stores information about the file (dimensions, colour depth, etc.) and makes the real file slightly **larger** than the calculated pixel data.
Example: 800 × 600 pixels at 24 bits = 11 520 000 bits = 1 440 000 bytes = **1.44 MB**.
A 1-bit image (two colours) is **24 times smaller** than a 24-bit image of the same size.
core.h: Calculating the size of an image file
core.p: A bitmap image is a grid of tiny squares called **pixels**, and each pixel is stored as a binary number that represents its colour. The number of bits used for each pixel is the **colour depth**. The total number of pixels is the **resolution**, found by multiplying the width by the height. So the data for the picture is: **file size (bits) = width in pixels × height in pixels × colour depth (bits per pixel)**. Real image files also store **metadata** (such as the width, height, colour depth, and sometimes the date or camera settings), which adds a small amount to the size; the exam questions usually say to ignore it or ask you to mention it as a reason the real file is slightly bigger.

bullets: **Sample** = a measurement of the amplitude of the sound wave at one instant.
**Sample rate** = number of samples per second, in Hz (CD quality is **44 100 Hz**).
**Bit depth** = number of bits used to store each sample (CD quality is **16 bits**).
**Duration must be in seconds**: change minutes to seconds first (3 minutes = 180 seconds).
**File size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration (s)**, then ÷ 8 for bytes.
A higher sample rate or bit depth records the wave **more accurately** (better quality) but makes the file **bigger**.
core.h: Calculating the size of a sound file
core.p: Sound in the real world is a continuous wave, so it has to be **sampled**: at regular intervals the amplitude (height) of the wave is measured and stored as a binary number. The number of samples taken each second is the **sample rate**, measured in **hertz (Hz)**, and the number of bits used to store each sample is the **bit depth**. The file size depends on all three of sample rate, bit depth and how long the recording lasts. **File size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration (in seconds)**. If the recording has more than one channel (stereo has two), multiply by the number of channels as well, but only if the question tells you to.

bullets: **Total storage = size of one file × number of files.**
**Number of files that fit = capacity ÷ file size**, rounded **down** to a whole number.
Convert both values to the **same unit** (for example both in MB) before dividing.
Example: a 16 GB card = 16 000 MB; photos of 2.4 MB each: 16 000 ÷ 2.4 = 6666.67, so **6666 photos** fit.
To check whether a set of files fits, **add the sizes**, then compare with the capacity.
Remember the operating system and other files also use space, so real capacity is slightly less than the stated amount.
core.p: Exam questions often ask whether files will fit on a device, or how much storage a collection of files needs. The method is to work out the **size of one file**, multiply by the **number of files**, convert everything into **one unit**, and then compare it with the capacity. If the question asks how many files fit on a device, divide the capacity by the file size and **round down** because you cannot store part of a file. Always convert so both numbers use the same unit before dividing.

bullets: Doubling the **sample rate** or **bit depth** doubles the file size, and gives a more accurate recording.
Doubling **width and height** together gives **4×** the pixels, so 4× the file size.
Reducing **colour depth** (e.g. 24-bit to 8-bit) makes the file **3 times smaller** but fewer colours are available, so images may look banded.
Reducing **resolution** makes the image less detailed (pixelated) and the file smaller.
Reducing the **sample rate** loses high frequencies and makes the sound less true to the original.
A smaller file **downloads faster**, uses **less bandwidth** and takes **less storage**.
core.h: How changing settings changes the file size and quality
core.p: Because the formulas are products, changing one factor changes the file size in direct proportion. **Doubling any one factor doubles the file size**: doubling the duration of a sound doubles the size, doubling the colour depth of an image doubles the size, and so on. Doubling both the width and the height of an image makes the file **four times** bigger because the number of pixels is multiplied by 2 × 2. The trade-off is always between **quality and size**: more pixels, more colours or more samples give a better representation of the original but need more storage and take longer to transfer.

bullets: **Step 1:** write the formula (for example size = width × height × colour depth).
**Step 2:** substitute the values, converting minutes to seconds and any other units first.
**Step 3:** calculate the result in **bits**.
**Step 4:** divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1000 for each step up to KB, MB or GB.
**Step 5:** write the final answer **with its unit**, and round only at the end.
If you run out of time, write the formula and substitution: these usually earn **method marks** even if the final answer is wrong.
core.h: A reliable method for exam calculations
core.p: Calculation questions in the OCR paper are marked by method, so a clear layout both prevents mistakes and secures the marks. First write the formula you are using, then substitute the numbers from the question, then work out the answer in bits, then convert to the units asked for, and finally write the answer with its unit. Check the units given in the question (is it asking for bytes, KB or MB?) and the units of the numbers you are given (minutes need converting to seconds, KB may need converting to bytes).

bullets: **Compression:** reducing file size so files need less storage and transfer faster (see lossy and lossless compression).
**Transmission time = file size in bits ÷ data transfer rate in bits per second** (for example 11 520 000 bits ÷ 8 000 000 bits per second = **1.44 s**).
**Choosing storage:** capacity needed for the files decides whether you need a USB stick, SSD, HDD or cloud storage.
**Hexadecimal:** one hex digit = 1 nibble (4 bits); two hex digits = 1 byte.
**Networks:** larger files use more bandwidth, so a slower connection takes longer to download them.
**Character sets:** more bits per character means a larger text file but a larger range of symbols.
core.p: The calculations here link to many other parts of the specification. File size determines how much **secondary storage** is needed and how long a file takes to **transmit over a network**, and it is the reason **compression** exists. It also connects to **binary and hexadecimal** (a byte is two hex digits, a nibble is one) and to **data representation** of characters, images and sound. Being able to link ideas is what lifts a 6-mark answer from level 2 to level 3.

exam: **State/give (1 mark):** units questions such as 'How many bits are in a byte?' are single-mark recall: write just '8'. Learn the order bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.

**Calculate (2 to 4 marks):** write the formula, substitute, calculate in bits, convert and finish with the **unit**. Typical split: 1 mark for the multiplication, 1 for ÷ 8, 1 for the final unit conversion.
**'Show your working':** if you have the formula and substitution right you can score method marks even with a wrong final answer, so always write it down.
**Convert first:** a classic trap is a duration in minutes or a file size in different units; mark schemes often award a mark for correctly converting to seconds or the common unit.
**Explain (2 marks):** 'Explain why a larger sample rate gives a bigger file': more samples are taken each second (1), and each sample needs the same number of bits, so more bits are stored (1).
**Describe the effect (3 marks):** mention the factor, the effect on file size (increases in proportion) and the effect on quality or detail (more detail/accuracy but needs more storage).
**Number of colours:** 'How many colours can 8 bits represent?' Answer 2^8 = 256; show the power of 2 for the mark.
**How many files fit?** Divide capacity by file size in the same unit and round **down**.
**Useful model phrases:** 'the file size is the number of bits per pixel multiplied by the number of pixels', 'more bits per sample means a more accurate representation of the sound wave'.
**Link to metadata:** if asked why the actual file is larger than your calculation, say it also stores **metadata** (such as dimensions and colour depth).
**Check plausibility:** a short text file should be bytes or KB, a photo MB, a film GB; if your answer is wildly off, recheck the ÷ 8 and ÷ 1000 steps.

mistakes.r: Use 1 KB = 1000 bytes (OCR) unless the question gives a different conversion; always follow the conversion in the question.
mistakes.w: Dividing by 1024 when the question has not said to.

mistakes.r: The formulas give an answer in bits; divide by 8 to get bytes before converting to KB or MB.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to divide by 8 to change bits into bytes.

mistakes.r: Duration must be in seconds; convert 3 minutes to 180 seconds first.
mistakes.w: Using minutes in the sound formula (e.g. 3 × 44 100 × 16).

mistakes.r: Resolution is width × height; the number of pixels is a product, not a sum.
mistakes.w: Adding width and height of an image instead of multiplying.

mistakes.r: Convert both to the same unit first (16 GB = 16 000 MB) and then divide.
mistakes.w: Mixing units, e.g. dividing 16 GB by 2.4 MB without converting.

mistakes.r: State the unit asked for (bits, bytes, KB, MB) and make sure the number matches it.
mistakes.w: Giving a final answer with no unit, or in the wrong unit.

mistakes.r: Round down, because a part-file cannot be stored (6666.67 means 6666 files).
mistakes.w: Rounding up the number of files that fit on a device.

mistakes.r: Bit = 1 binary digit, nibble = 4 bits, byte = 8 bits.
mistakes.w: Saying a bit is 'a byte' or a nibble is '8 bits'.

mistakes.r: Doubling both the width and the height gives four times as many pixels, so four times the file size.
mistakes.w: Saying that doubling the width and height doubles the file size.

summary: OCR J277 1.2 asks you to know the units of data storage (bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB), convert between them, and calculate the file size and storage capacity needed for text, images and sound. These calculation questions appear regularly on Paper 1 and are mostly method marks, so a clear step-by-step approach is worth many easy marks.

terms.d: A single binary digit, either 0 or 1; the smallest unit of data in a computer.
A group of 4 bits; half a byte.
A group of 8 bits; the basic unit for measuring file size and storage.
The smallest individual element of a bitmap image, each stored as a binary value for its colour.
The number of pixels in an image, found by multiplying its width by its height in pixels.
The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel in an image.
Data about a file, such as its dimensions, colour depth or date, that is stored with it.
A measurement of the amplitude of a sound wave taken at one point in time.
The number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The number of bits used to store each sound sample.
A defined list of characters, each with its own unique binary code (for example ASCII or Unicode).
The maximum amount of data a storage device or memory can hold.
1024 bytes (2^10 bytes); the binary-prefix unit sometimes confused with a kilobyte.

worked.q: A bitmap image is 800 pixels wide and 600 pixels high with a colour depth of 24 bits. Calculate the file size in megabytes (ignore metadata). [3 marks]
steps: File size = width × height × colour depth.

worked.q: A song is recorded in mono with a sample rate of 44 100 Hz and a bit depth of 16 bits. It lasts 3 minutes. Calculate the file size in megabytes. [4 marks]
steps: Bits = sample rate × bit depth × duration = 44 100 × 16 × 180.

worked.q: A 16 GB memory card is used to store photos that are each 2.4 MB. How many photos can the card hold? [3 marks]
steps: Convert to the same unit: 16 GB × 1000 = 16 000 MB.
Number of photos = capacity ÷ file size = 16 000 ÷ 2.4 = 6666.67.
A part-photo cannot be stored, so round down.
